content.text: When we heat a substance, we transfer energy to it. But what exactly is this energy? Internal energy describes the total energy stored within a substance due to the motion and arrangement of its particles. It's the microscopic explanation for temperature and heat.

Internal energy = total kinetic energy of all particles + total potential energy of all particles. Kinetic energy is related to particle motion (and therefore temperature), while potential energy is related to the bonds and forces between particles.

Students often confuse temperature and internal energy. Temperature measures the average kinetic energy per particle, while internal energy is the total energy (kinetic + potential) of all particles. Two objects at the same temperature can have very different internal energies.

During a change of state, kinetic energy stays constant (temperature does not change) while potential energy changes (bonds are broken or formed). This is why the internal energy still increases during melting or boiling even though the temperature stays the same.
Explain why temperature stays constant during melting even though energy is being added.
Energy is absorbed from the surroundings
This energy breaks bonds between particles in the solid
The energy increases the potential energy of particles, not their kinetic energy
Since temperature depends on average kinetic energy, and KE doesn't change, temperature stays constant
All the energy goes into changing the structure (solid → liquid), not speeding up particles
Two containers have equal masses of water. Container A is at 20°C and container B is at 80°C. Compare their internal energies.
Container B has more internal energy because:
Both have the same number of particles (same mass)
But container B is at a higher temperature
Higher temperature means particles have greater average kinetic energy
Total kinetic energy is higher, so internal energy is higher
A cup of hot tea and a bathtub of warm water are at 70°C and 40°C respectively. Which has more internal energy?
The bathtub has more internal energy, even though it's at a lower temperature.
The bathtub contains far more water (more particles)
Total internal energy depends on the number of particles AND their average energy
More particles = more total energy, even if each particle has less KE on average
Explain what happens to the internal energy of water as ice at -10°C is heated to steam at 110°C.

Comparing Heat, Temperature, and Internal Energy
Total KE + PE of all particles
Energy transfer due to temp difference
A spark has high temperature but low internal energy (few particles)
A bathtub has lower temperature but higher internal energy (many particles)
Heat is a transfer process; internal energy and temperature describe states
Different substances store different amounts of internal energy per degree of temperature change. This is why water takes longer to heat than metal.
When two objects are in contact, heat flows until they reach the same temperature (thermal equilibrium). Internal energy is transferred from the hotter to the cooler object.
Materials that absorb/release large amounts of energy during state changes are used for:
Heat storage (store energy when melting, release when freezing)
— Temperature is a measure of average KE; heat is energy transfer due to temperature difference.
— Size determines total internal energy, not temperature. A tiny spark is hotter than a cold bath, despite having less internal energy.
— It includes both kinetic AND potential energy of particles.
"If temperature is constant, internal energy is constant"
— Not during state changes! Internal energy increases during melting/boiling even though temperature doesn't.
— All objects above absolute zero have internal energy. "Cold" objects just have less than "hot" ones.

Internal energy is the total kinetic energy and total potential energy of all the particles in a substance.

The kinetic energy component arises from the random motion or vibration of particles, and the potential energy component arises from the forces (bonds) between particles. (explanation with physics reasoning)
During boiling, the energy supplied breaks bonds between liquid particles rather than increasing their speed.

The potential energy of the particles increases as they move further apart and become gas, but their average kinetic energy (and therefore temperature) remains unchanged. Internal energy increases because potential energy increases. (explanation with physics reasoning)

Same temperature means same average kinetic energy per particle, but internal energy is the total KE + PE of all particles. An object with more mass (more particles) will have greater total internal energy even at the same temperature. (explanation with physics reasoning)
100 g of water at 80°C has more internal energy.
Both have the same mass (same number of particles), but at 80°C the particles have greater average kinetic energy. (comparison)
200 g of water at 40°C has more internal energy.
Although its temperature is lower (less KE per particle), it has four times as many particles, giving a much larger total internal energy. (comparison)

Steam at 100°C carries additional latent heat of vaporisation.

When steam contacts skin it first condenses, releasing about 2260 J per gram of latent heat. Then the resulting water at 100°C cools further, releasing more energy. Water at 100°C can only release energy as it cools. So steam transfers much more total energy to the skin, causing a more severe burn. (explanation with physics reasoning)
